new_statements.quote: Stress, which is rather light in Wambon, generally falls on the penultimate syllable; in some words we found the stress on the final and the penultimate syllable in variation. Example:/tambúlop/ 'kind of fruit'; /tambulóp/ 'kind of fruit'. Due to insufficient data on stress phenomena, it is impossible to state how these cases of variable stress affect the predictability of stress in Wambon.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Rendered PDF page 26 of (image scan, 112 pp., extracted text returns nothing) and read it as an image: it is book p. 12, running head 'The Morphology of Wambon', section '2.2 Syllables and words'. The passage is there verbatim: 'Stress, which is rather light in Wambon, generally falls on the penultimate syllable; in some words we found the stress on the final and the penultimate syllable in variation. Example:/tambúlop/ 'kind of fruit'; /tambulóp/ 'kind of fruit'. Due to insufficient data on stress phenomena, it is impossible to state how these cases of variable stress affect the predictability of stress in Wambon.' The saved scanned file garbles the accents…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Digul-Wambon stress is weak and normally on the penultimate syllable; a minority of words fluctuate between penultimate and final stress, and the authors decline to state a rule beyond the penultimate default.
new_statements.exceptions: Some words show free variation between penultimate and final stress (tambúlop ~ tambulóp 'kind of fruit'); authors say data on stress are insufficient to assess predictability.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word, canonical shape (C)V(C).{CV(C)}0-5, max six syllables); stress described as phonetically light. IDENTITY CAVEAT: this describes Digul-Wambon (Manggelum/Sawagit area; ISO wms), a sister variety of Ketum in Glottolog's Ketum-Wambon node, not Ketum itself. The only Ketum-specific data found (Lebold et al. 2014 Appendix C, Arimbit wordlist) mark stress with mixed placement (many disyllables final-stressed: ɑmˈbɑr, keˈrop, seˈrun, kɑˈrit, kəˈnop; others initial: ˈbɑŋgɑr, ˈmuŋgup, ˈnɑtum, ˈsɑɾip) and contain no statement.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is about Digul-Wambon (ISO 639-3 wms; Manggelum/Sawagit area on the upper Digul), the sister languoid of Ketum inside Glottolog's Ketum-Wambon node (ketu1239); Ketum (ktt; Arimbit, Kuken, part of Bayanggop; locally 'Mandobo Utara' / 'Ketum-Manop') has only 49% apparent lexical similarity with Wambon/Manggelum in Lebold et al. 2014, whose authors leave open whether it is a Wambon dialect or a separate language; Jang 2003 (per de Vries et al. 2012: 271) treats it as 'Ketum Wambon', a minor grouping of Wambon; Wikipedia folds it into North/Digul Wambon. No phonological description of Ketum itself exists in anything found. If the catalog accepts the Wambon statement it should be filed under Wambon (wms), not ketu1238.

new_statements.quote: While Mountain Ok languages are described as tonal (Telefol, Tifal, Mian), in Lowland Ok and Greater Awyu languages it is not the tone contour but lexical stress that seems to be distinctive. [p. 2] ... Both languages [Muyu and Mandobo] have distinctive lexical stress, as is true for all other Awyu-Dumut languages and some other Ok languages. [p. 18, sec. 6.2 'Typology']

Both sentences are verbatim in the scanned file at printed p. 2 ('..in Lowland Ok and Greater Awyu languages it is not the tone con-tour but lexical stress that seems to be distinctive.') and printed p. 18 sec. 6.2 TYPOLOGY ('Both languages have distinctive lexical stress, as is true for all other Awyu-Dumut languages and some other Ok languages.'); the only difference is A's inserted gloss '[Muyu and Mandobo]' and the '[p. 2]..' joiner; the clipped extracted text also shows both (lines 104, 961). Reading…
new_statements.relation_note: Two sentences: Greater Awyu languages are not tonal; lexical stress seems distinctive in Lowland Ok and Greater Awyu; all Awyu-Dumut languages have distinctive lexical stress. Rest of the phonology paragraph: inventories <= 15 consonants and 7 vowels, Kombai complex vowels, no vowel length contrast in Greater Awyu.
new_statements.rule_in_words: According to this comparative overview, Greater Awyu (and specifically all Awyu-Dumut) languages are non-tonal and have lexical stress that 'seems to be distinctive'; no placement rule is given and no language-by-language evidence is cited.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the hedge 'seems to be distinctive' is the authors' own. Note the tension with the first-hand Dumut sources held by the project: de Vries & Wiersma 1992 (Digul Wambon: light stress, generally penultimate, some penult~final variation) and van den Heuvel 2025 (Yonggom Wambon: weak, predictable final-syllable stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Family-level generalization: the two sentences quantify over 'Greater Awyu languages' and 'all other Awyu-Dumut languages', a set that includes Ketum by classification (Greater Awyu > Awyu-Dumut > Dumut > Ketum-Wambon), but Ketum/Kitum is never named in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text: no hit; the Dumut data used are Digul Wambon, Yonggom Wambon and Mandobo/Kaeti). Second-hand typological summary, not a first-hand description of Ketum. Glottolog lists this article on the ketu1238 page (ref 321966) for classification.
